# HDR QR Code

:::lead
**Here’s an HDR [QR Code](QRCode).** If you’re viewing this on an Apple device’s built-in display, it should work. If the big QR code is brighter than the smaller one, it works.
:::

<div style="display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: 1em; align-items: flex-end;" class="not-prose">
<div style="position: relative; background: black; width: 240px; height: 240px;">
<video
  ref="vid"
  @canplaythrough="loaded"
  poster="data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAABAAAAAQAQAAAAA3iMLMAAAAAXNSR0IArs4c6QAAAA5JREFUeNpj+P+fgRQEAP1OH+HeyHWXAAAAAElFTkSuQmCC"
  src="data:video/mp4;base64,"
  muted
  autoplay
  playsinline
  style="
    position: absolute;
    top: 0;
    left: 0;
    width: 100%;
    height: 100%;
  "
></video>
<img style="display:block;position:absolute;top:0;left:0;width:100%;height:100%" src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Reference">
</div>

<div style="width: 120px">
<small style="display: block; line-height: 1.25; margin-bottom: 1ex;"><strong>normal qr code</strong><br>for reference</small>
<img style="background:white;display:block" src="data:image/png;base64," alt="Reference" width="120">
</div>
</div>

For the example to work, your platform, your browser, and your display must support displaying HDR content. Also, low-power mode must be turned off. These setups have been tested to work:

- iPad Pro (M2), built-in display
- iPhone 13, built-in display
- MacBook Pro (M1), built-in display

**On a recent iPhone/iPad device, it appears to be [roughly ~7 times brighter](https://twitter.com/dtinth/status/1670438696871501825)**[^brighter].

[^brighter]: This is probably a flawed way to measure it, but I get this number by using a camera to take a photo of the screen. I set the ISO setting to be very low, so both QR codes appear as a shade of gray. I then compared the brightness of the two QR codes to obtain the ratio.

## Survey

Does it work on your device? Please fill out this survey:

<div style="height:800px;position:relative;display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;box-shadow:inset 0 0 5px #e9e8e7">
  <iframe :src="surveySrc" v-if="surveySrc" style="width:100%;height:100%;border:none;position:absolute;top:0;left:0"></iframe>
  <div v-if="!surveySrc">(Loading survey...)</div>
</div>

-->

<script>
  export default {
    setup() {
      const vid = Vue.ref()
      const surveySrc = Vue.ref()
      let played = false
      const go = () => {
        if (played) return
        vid.value.play()
        played = true
      }
      Vue.onMounted(() => {
        document.addEventListener('pointerdown', go)
        surveySrc.value = `https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLScda0Im0YQZULgY49GHitX8BJCNFb4Nr-6OFDALSTsZ-Fcl8Q/viewform?usp=pp_url&entry.1847535102=${navigator.userAgent}`
      })
      Vue.onUnmounted(() => {
        document.removeEventListener('pointerdown', go)
      })
      const loaded = () => {
        vid.value.currentTime = 0
      }
      return { vid, loaded, surveySrc }
    }
  }
</script>

## How it works

It works by displaying a [color](Colors) whose brightness is _way_ outside the standard range of sRGB color space.

Unfortunately, this color cannot be represented with CSS colors (`rgb(999,999,999)` doesn’t work) or any of the widely-supported image formats. However, an HDR video can represent this color.

**Therefore, the QR code you see above is actually a `<video>` containing very bright white pixels with a QR code overlaid on top.**

See: <https://github.com/dtinth/superwhite>
